edition.title: Morning Edition
edition.dek: Climate diplomacy's difficult final hours; a winter truce proposal; the energy shock; and the science of seeing what is hidden.

lead_story.headline: COP31 draft removes fossil-fuel language as summit approaches deadline
lead_story.summary: A revised negotiating draft in Antalya drops references to ending fossil-fuel use and an earlier adaptation-finance target. Turkey and Australia say they are seeking an agreement acceptable to nearly 200 countries; critics say the compromise is too weak. The text is not yet a final deal.
lead_story.why_it_matters: The negotiations test whether countries can turn climate pledges into a funded, actionable agreement despite deep differences over energy and finance.

items.headline: Ukraine and European allies seek a winter pause in attacks on energy infrastructure
items.summary: After talks in Berlin, Ukraine and European partners called on Russia to halt strikes on energy facilities and allow safer Black Sea food exports. The appeal is a proposal, not an agreed ceasefire.
items.why_it_matters: Civilian heating and electricity supplies are exposed as winter approaches, while European participation in negotiations remains a central diplomatic question.

items.headline: IEA says the Middle East war has permanently changed global energy security
items.summary: The International Energy Agency's new World Energy Outlook describes an unprecedented oil and gas supply shock linked to the Iran war and the Strait of Hormuz. It expects countries to diversify supply and accelerate some domestic energy investments; the long-term projections are scenarios, not certainties.
items.why_it_matters: The disruption affects transport, fertilizer, food prices and energy policy far beyond the Gulf.

items.headline: CERN experiment probes an exceptionally rare particle decay
items.summary: Researchers at the LHCb experiment report evidence of a rare beauty-particle decay involving two muons. The result so far agrees with the Standard Model rather than establishing new physics.
items.why_it_matters: Precision tests of very rare processes can reveal departures from current theory even when the first result confirms its predictions.

items.headline: Recent miss: Ukraine reports attacks on two Russian oil refineries
items.summary: Ukraine says its forces struck the Ilsky and Afipsky refineries in Krasnodar region, part of a campaign against fuel infrastructure. Independent battle-damage assessments remain limited.
items.why_it_matters: The attacks demonstrate the continuing pressure on energy logistics even as diplomatic talks seek a path to a ceasefire.

items.headline: Older catch-up: new imaging method brings faint exoplanets into view
items.summary: A Nature study published November 4 describes an image-processing method that models stellar glare and can reveal planets otherwise obscured in telescope data. Researchers tested it on James Webb Space Telescope observations; claims about future Earth-like planets remain prospective.
items.why_it_matters: Better processing can extract more information from existing observatories without waiting for entirely new telescopes.

items.headline: Older catch-up: Alaska site offers rare traces of life 13,800 years ago
items.summary: Excavations southeast of Fairbanks uncovered a hearth, possible shelter features, tools, needles and an antler ornament. Researchers interpret the finds as evidence of repeated occupation; some claims about the earliest dwelling remain provisional.
items.why_it_matters: The site helps reconstruct how early communities lived in Beringia beyond the familiar story of migration routes.

items.headline: A documentary remembers the people who keep outdoor hockey rinks alive
items.summary: A new film follows Canadian volunteers who maintain neighborhood outdoor ice rinks, including a longtime Newmarket rink-maker. A free community screening is planned for December 4.
items.why_it_matters: The story is about patient local work that makes a familiar winter gathering place possible.

items.headline: Is moral character more central to identity than memory?
items.summary: Psychologist Nina Strohminger argues that people's judgments of personal identity track changes in moral character more strongly than ordinary memory loss. Experiments illuminate how people judge continuity, not a definitive metaphysical answer to what a person is.
items.why_it_matters: The argument changes how we think about personality, responsibility and the meaning of remaining oneself.

worth_your_time.headline: How intuitions can be rational without being infallible
worth_your_time.summary: Philosopher Marc A. Moffett argues that ordinary intuitions can present possibilities and reasons much as perception presents physical surroundings. His account tries to explain why a feeling that something is wrong may count as evidence without being beyond challenge.
worth_your_time.why_it_matters: A careful account of intuition can distinguish useful judgment from overconfidence and prejudice.

reflection.passage: To affect the quality of the day, that is the highest of arts.
reflection.author: Henry David Thoreau
reflection.work: Walden, Where I Lived, and What I Lived For
reflection.context: Thoreau's experiment in deliberate living asks readers to attend to the shape of everyday experience rather than equate progress with speed or accumulation.
reflection.question: What would change the quality, rather than simply the productivity, of this day?

https://aeon.co/essays/moral-character-i.standfirst: Psychologist Nina Strohminger argues that people's judgments of personal identity track changes in moral character more strongly than ordinary memory loss. Experiments illuminate how people judge continuity, not a definitive metaphysical answer to what a person is.
body: Question: What makes someone the same person over time — memories, character, or something else?
Thesis: Strohminger argues that ordinary judgments of personal identity depend especially strongly on moral character, more than on generic episodic memory.

Reasoning: Experiments ask people to compare changes in memory, cognition, preferences and moral dispositions. Participants tend to judge a person as less like their former self when moral faculties change.
Concept: The account concerns how people attribute identity and maintain relationships; it is not a proof that metaphysical identity literally consists only of morality.
Example: A person who forgets a journey may still be recognized as themselves; a person whose treatment of loved ones becomes radically cruel may feel transformed despite remembering everything.
Background: John Locke famously tied personal identity to consciousness and memory. The essay challenges a simple popular reading of that tradition.
Objection: Judgments about who someone is may reflect which traits we value, not the persistence conditions of persons.
Possible response: The social purpose of identity concepts may help explain why moral dispositions matter so much to ordinary attribution.
Implication: Medical, legal and family decisions should distinguish a change in social recognition from a person's continuing rights and interests.
Open questions: Would different cultures or first-person accounts produce the same pattern? Can moral traits be separated cleanly from memory and circumstance?

https://aeon.co/essays/sometimes-you-jus.standfirst: Philosopher Marc A. Moffett argues that ordinary intuitions can present possibilities and reasons much as perception presents physical surroundings. His account tries to explain why a feeling that something is wrong may count as evidence without being beyond challenge.
body: Question: Can an immediate sense that something is wrong provide rational grounds for belief?
Thesis: Moffett argues that intuition has a presentational role analogous to perception: it can make a conceptual or normative possibility appear salient without a conscious chain of inference.
Argument: We often act on judgments before we can list reasons, just as we see a tree without inferring it from patches of color.
Example: Someone senses a phishing email is suspicious, or a philosopher immediately judges a fake-barn case problematic. The author sees a common cognitive capacity across these cases.
Background: Epistemology distinguishes the psychological origin of a belief from its justification. The essay draws on philosophical accounts of perceptual seeming and rational intuition.
Objection: Intuitions can encode bias, fear, or unreliable habits; apparent immediacy alone cannot establish truth.
Response: Treating intuitions as potentially reason-giving does not make them infallible. They remain open to criticism and correction by evidence.
Implication: Deliberation may require evaluating intuitions rather than dismissing them as irrational or treating them as verdicts.
Connections: Thought experiments, expert perception, phenomenology and everyday practical judgment all raise questions about what counts as evidence.
Unresolved: How can we tell trained intuition from prejudice? When should explicit evidence override a strong seeming?
